sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.markdown: **No state license covers chimney work — or any home improvement work — in New York.** The **NY Department of State states: "NYS does not license home improvement contractors, however, some counties and local municipalities do"** (DOS consumer alert, Apr 18, 2023), naming **New York City, Buffalo, and Suffolk, Nassau, Westchester, Putnam, and Rockland counties**. Oversight is a **municipal/county patchwork**: **NYC** (Dept. of Consumer & Worker Protection — HIC license; one principal must pass DCWP's Home Improvement Exam, 30 questions, 21 correct to pass, and the applicant must enroll in the Trust Fund or post a $20,000 surety bond — DCWP license checklist, checked Sep 25, 2026), the five counties, and **Buffalo** each run their own HIC licensing; many towns and villages add their own registration. Where a locality requires a license, **an unlicensed contractor generally cannot enforce the contract or sue to recover payment** — real homeowner leverage, but only inside those borders. Elsewhere (much of upstate), **there may be nothing to check.** "Licensed" in NY marketing means "licensed in the city/county where they work," not statewide.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Widest of the Northeast. Even NYC's exam is a general home-improvement/business test — **nothing chimney-specific** — and outside the licensed counties there is no credential at all. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) and an independent audit fill a genuine vacuum, especially upstate.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV — high confidence; loophole just closed)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.markdown: **The Property Condition Disclosure Act (Real Property Law Art. 14, §§ 460–467; form at § 462) became genuinely mandatory only on March 20, 2024.** From 2002 until then, sellers could hand buyers a **$500 credit and skip the form entirely** — and nearly all did. **Chapter 484 of the Laws of 2023 (S5400/A1967, signed Sept 22, 2023, effective 180 days later)** **deleted the $500 credit** (§ 465 retitled "Remedy" → "Liability"; a seller is now liable for actual damages for a willful failure), repealed § 467, and added flood questions. The statutory form in § 462 (text last revised July 2025 on the Senate site) asks known-condition Yes/No/Unkn/NA items including **"Chimney/fireplace or stove?" (item 50)** and **"Heating system?" (item 54)** — actual-knowledge standard, no inspection required to answer. **No inspection is mandated at transfer**; NFPA 211 Level 2-at-sale stays a NATIONAL STANDARD, not NY law.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: **General Business Law § 349** and **§ 350 (false advertising)** give a private right of action, but the treble is **weak and discretionary — "three times the actual damages up to one thousand dollars"** for willful/knowing violations, plus discretionary attorney's fees (contrast NJ's mandatory treble). **2026 change:** the **FAIR Business Practices Act (S8416, signed Dec 19, 2025; Ch. 708 of 2025 per the Senate bill page; effective 60 days after signing)** rewrote § 349(a) to declare "Unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices" unlawful — but the **private action in § 349(h) still reaches only deceptive acts**, with the same $50-minimum / $1,000-capped treble; the new "unfair" and "abusive" prongs are AG-enforced. Home improvement contracts are separately governed by **GBL Article 36-A (§§ 770–776)**: written contract required, with a **3-business-day right to cancel** (owner may cancel until midnight of the third business day after signing, GBL § 771; emergency-waiver exception in the owner's handwriting). The AG (ag.ny.gov) and local consumer-affairs offices take complaints; NYC DCWP is unusually active. Hiring outside the licensing regime can forfeit contract-enforcement leverage.

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV — medium-high; two-cycle + NYC carve-out)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: Statewide **Uniform Fire Prevention & Building Code**; the **2025 Residential Code of New York State (a derivative of the 2024 IRC) took effect December 31, 2025** as part of the 2025 Uniform Code — permit applications from that date must comply (the 2020 RCNYS/2018 IRC is superseded). Chapter 10 governs masonry and factory-built chimneys and fireplaces. **NYC is exempt and runs its own NYC Construction Codes** (solid-fuel appliances tightly restricted under Title 27). Relines, rebuilds, and appliance installs are generally permit work through the local building department; sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not. Local variation is real — say so.

sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **Amanda's Law (Executive Law § 378(5-a), as amended by Chapter 367 of the Laws of 2009; in effect 2010)** requires that "every one or two-family dwelling, or any dwelling accommodation located in a building owned as a condominium or cooperative in the state or any multiple dwellings shall have installed an operable carbon monoxide detector," but "only where the dwelling unit has appliances, devices or systems that may emit carbon monoxide or has an attached garage." The Uniform Code rule implementing it (described by the NYS Department of Health) extends to townhouses and applies **"without regard to the date of construction or sale"** — that phrase is the rule's, not the statute's. Broad coverage, but enforced as a standing requirement rather than a NJ-style pre-sale certificate. A permitted chimney job is still the natural moment to verify alarms.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban regime; NYC restricts new solid-fuel installations under its own code. Upstate wood-heat density is high. Not a major content section outside NYC's install limits.

sections.rawHeading: 8 · Scam landscape (GOV — one historical action confirmed)
sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: NY AG and NYC DCWP both have active home-improvement-fraud enforcement histories, and the phone/door "cheap cleaning, then scary repair" pitch is the textbook GBL Art. 36-A / § 349 scenario. **Confirmed public action (allegations, 2005):** on Dec 12, 2005 the NY AG sued Flue Season, Inc. and All American Service Maintenance, Inc. (and previously operated entities including Chimney Care Corp. and Big Apple Chimney Sweeps, Inc.), alleging operators targeted elderly residents with low-ball cleaning offers, then used scare tactics about chimney fires/back-drafts to sell $1,200–$3,000 repairs and denied the legally required cooling-off period (Do Not Call Law; Home Improvement Contracts Law). The release describes a lawsuit — **present it as alleged, and do not state an outcome** (not verified). Frame it as a pattern with a 20-year history, not a current accusation.

sections.title: Season calendar
sections.markdown: Cold statewide; longer/lake-effect upstate. Burn season ~Oct–Apr. Rush: SEP–NOV. Best booking: APR–JUN. NYC market milder and year-rounder.

sections.title: Price seeding (internal)
sections.markdown: NYC metro + Westchester/Long Island run **well above national**; upstate near or below national. Regionalize sharply within the state.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: New York is the **patchwork state**: no statewide license, so protection depends entirely on which city or county you're in — NYC and the big suburban counties license and test; much of upstate licenses nothing. **The gap between "licensed in NYC" and "licensed in New York" is the whole page.** The second beat is the 2024 disclosure fix: for two decades sellers paid $500 to reveal nothing about the chimney; that door just closed. But NY's consumer-fraud damages ($1,000-capped, discretionary) are far weaker than neighboring NJ — protection here lives in *local licensing* and *contract-enforcement forfeiture*, not in the damages statute.

faq.q: What should I check before hiring a chimney company in New York?
faq.a: State licensing: NO state license — LOCAL patchwork (NYC/Nassau/Suffolk/Westchester/Putnam/Rockland/Buffalo). Registration or credential: local only. Seller disclosure at sale: YES — mandatory since Mar 20, 2024 (Ch. 484 of 2023), "Chimney/fireplace or stove?" item 50 (RPL § 462). Right to cancel a sale made at your home: YES (GBL § 771). Carbon monoxide alarm law: broad (Amanda's Law, Exec. Law § 378(5-a)). Where to check a contractor: local consumer-affairs registries (NYC DCWP, county offices) + ag.ny.gov complaints. Then ask the eight questions below, get the inspection findings in writing with photos, and never sign for "emergency" work on the day of a door-knock.
